study_id: Yoon et al. - 2018 - Personalized survival predictions via Trees of Predictors An application to cardiac transplantation

eligibility.Eligibility Rationale: The study analyzes adult heart transplant candidates and recipients using a non‑linear machine learning method (Trees of Predictors) to predict post‑ and pre‑transplant survival, meeting all population, intervention, outcome, and study design criteria.

identification_methods.Sponsorship source: Office of Naval Research (ONR) and National Science Foundation (NSF)
identification_methods.Setting: Retrospective cohort using UNOS registry data
identification_methods.Comments: Open access article; uses United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) database of heart transplant patients from 1985-2015
identification_methods.Identification Notes: Included adults >18 years; excluded patients <18; final cohorts 51,971 transplanted and 30,911 wait-listed patients
identification_methods.AI Model Architecture: Trees of Predictors (ToPs) with base learners Cox Regression, Linear Perceptron, Logistic Regression
identification_methods.Comparator: Clinical risk scores (DRI, IMPACT, RSS) and state-of-the-art machine learning methods
identification_methods.Input Variables: 53 selected features (33 recipient, 14 donor, 6 donor-recipient compatibility) after discarding high-missing features
identification_methods.Missing Data Handling: Multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) with 10 imputations; discarded features with >10% missing
identification_methods.Methods Notes: Tree of predictors creates clusters and assigns specific predictive models; predictions aggregated via weighted average using linear perceptron; addresses heterogeneity across patients and time horizons

population.Inclusion criteria: Patients registered for heart transplantation in the UNOS database (1985-2015) who are adults (age ≥18)
population.Exclusion criteria: Patients age <18; features with >10% missing data; post-transplantation only features
population.Target Population: Heart transplant recipients and wait-listed patients
population.Population Notes: Data split into 5-fold cross-validation with 80% training and 20% testing; cohorts: 51,971 transplanted and 30,911 wait-listed after exclusions

interventions_outcomes.Intervention Input Data Modality: Tabular clinical features from UNOS database
interventions_outcomes.Feature Selection Method: Relevance scores based on correlation coefficient; discarding features with >10% missing
interventions_outcomes.Temporal Handling: Static baseline data with separate models for each time horizon (3‑month, 1‑year, 3‑year, 10‑year)
interventions_outcomes.Interventions Notes: Tree of predictors that clusters patients and assigns specific base learners (Cox Regression, Linear Perceptron, Logistic Regression) to each cluster; 5‑fold cross‑validation
interventions_outcomes.Reported outcomes in study: Survival prediction AUC and C‑index at multiple horizons (3‑month, 1‑year, 3‑year, 10‑year) post‑ and pre‑transplantation
interventions_outcomes.Outcomes Notes: Focus on AUC improvements over clinical risk scores and other ML methods
interventions_outcomes.Result data Notes: Tables report AUC values (e.g., 0.660 for 3‑month post‑transplantation) and C‑index; statistically significant improvements (p < 0.01)
interventions_outcomes.Primary Outcome group: All transplanted patients in the test set
interventions_outcomes.Primary Outcome Metric Definition: Area under ROC curve for predicting survival at 3 months post‑transplantation
interventions_outcomes.Primary Outcome Notes: Significant improvement over RSS; AUC increase from 0.587 to 0.660
